clue.text: Telephone touch may display engaged signal?

definitions.note: a descriptive phrase for the finger that wears an engagement ring

blocks.note: to ring someone is to telephone them
to finger something is to touch it

explanation.surface: Someone tapping a phone screen and seeing the line is busy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Engaged signal' suggests the busy tone on a phone line; here engaged means betrothed, and the signal is the ring.
explanation.definitionFit: The fourth finger of the left hand traditionally carries an engagement ring, announcing that its wearer is betrothed.

clue.text: Development of Geoff's hooter

indicators.note: the answer is made of, or comes out of, the run of letters in the next words

blocks.note: the letters run across the gap from the end of the name into the start of the next word

explanation.surface: How Geoff's big nose came about.
explanation.walkthrough: Hooter is British slang for a nose, which makes the surface read like an odd medical history.
explanation.definitionFit: An offshoot is a branch or later growth that develops from something larger, such as a side project.

clue.text: Vehicle oily, but not starting in a very active way

indicators.note: a word that is not starting has had its first letter removed

blocks.note: a bus is a road vehicle
taken as written before its opening letter goes

explanation.surface: A greasy vehicle that is nonetheless whizzing about.
explanation.definitionFit: Busily is the adverb from busy, describing someone working energetically and with plenty to do.

clue.text: Dead Queen wrapped in flannelette

indicators.note: the answer is enclosed, like a parcel, within the letters of the following word

blocks.note: sits in the middle of the fabric's name

explanation.surface: A late monarch laid out in a soft cotton shroud.
explanation.walkthrough: Queen Anne reigned in Britain from 1702 to 1714; 'Queen Anne's dead' is an old saying for stale news.
explanation.definitionFit: Anne was a British monarch who died in 1714, so she is a queen of the past.

clue.text: Garland for girl asked to answer on linked circles

indicators.note: in a down entry one part placed on another sits directly above it

blocks.note: the old song begins 'Daisy, Daisy, give me your answer, do'
a chain is a series of linked rings

explanation.surface: A garland offered to a girl who is pressed to reply about some interlocking rings.
explanation.walkthrough: The song is 'Daisy Bell' (A Bicycle Built for Two), in which the singer begs Daisy for an answer to his proposal.
explanation.definitionFit: A daisy chain is a string of daisies threaded stem to flower, worn as a garland or necklace.

clue.text: Bride or groom just sitting on rising dew

indicators.note: in a down entry a word that is rising reads from the bottom upwards
in a down entry the first part sits above, on top of, the second

blocks.note: just and newly both mean recently
taken as written, then turned upwards

explanation.surface: A wedding guest perched on wet morning grass.
explanation.definitionFit: Either partner in a couple who have only recently married is a newlywed.

clue.text: Yorkshire pudding for cricketer?

blocks.note: first meaning: the egg, flour and milk mixture that is baked into this dish
second meaning: the player who wields the bat

explanation.surface: A Yorkshire cricket club's tea menu.
explanation.walkthrough: A Yorkshire pudding is a baked savoury pudding served with British roast beef; it is made from batter. Yorkshire is also a famous cricketing county.
explanation.definitionFit: Batter is the liquid mix of flour, eggs and milk for the pudding, and also a player facing the bowler.

clue.text: It's a legal document any way

indicators.note: read in any direction, forwards or back, the word comes out unchanged

blocks.note: a signed contract conveying property

explanation.surface: Someone insisting a paper is binding whichever way you look at it.
explanation.definitionFit: A deed is a written, signed instrument that transfers property or binds parties in law.

clue.text: Disease in Channel, plus one east of New Zealand

indicators.note: in an across entry anything east of something else is placed to its right

blocks.note: taken as written
a flue is a duct or channel for smoke
standard abbreviation of the country
a means one, as in a single item

explanation.surface: An illness spreading in the English Channel and beyond New Zealand.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Channel' looks like the English Channel; it is a chimney duct.
explanation.definitionFit: Influenza is the viral illness more usually called flu, bringing fever and aches.

clue.text: Remove all trace of king kept in comfort

indicators.note: something kept in another thing is held inside it

blocks.note: R stands for Rex, Latin for king
ease is comfort or relief

explanation.surface: A pampered monarch kept in luxury vanishes without a trace.
explanation.definitionFit: To erase is to rub out or delete so completely that nothing is left behind.

clue.text: Heater makes the rig safe

indicators.note: the following letters are made into, or fashioned into, something new

blocks.note: the letters of the last two words; 'the' is part of the surface

explanation.surface: Fitting a heater makes an oil rig safe.
explanation.definitionFit: A gas fire is a room heater burning mains gas, common in British homes.

clue.text: Acknowledged what played music in blue?

indicators.note: one part is set inside the other

blocks.note: a lute is a stringed instrument
feeling blue is feeling sad

explanation.surface: Recognising a performer of mournful blues.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Music in blue' hints at the blues; blue is a mood here.
explanation.definitionFit: To salute someone is to greet or recognise them formally, so saluted means greeted in recognition.

clue.text: I almost row to New York, which could be dramatic!

definitions.note: a description: dramatic irony is a kind of it

indicators.note: almost all of a word means it stops one letter short

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written, then cut short
standard abbreviation of the city and state

explanation.surface: A rower boasting of nearly crossing the Atlantic to New York, quite a story.
explanation.walkthrough: Dramatic irony is when an audience knows something a character does not.
explanation.definitionFit: Irony comes in several kinds, and dramatic irony is a well known theatrical one.

clue.text: The wrong way to support charges

blocks.note: to back someone is to support them
wards are people in one's care, one's charges

explanation.surface: Bad advice on how to back up criminal charges.
explanation.definitionFit: Going backwards means moving in reverse, the opposite of the usual direction.

clue.text: Imploring person standing around to visit child

indicators.note: standing around something means surrounding it on all sides

blocks.note: a being is a living person
to see someone can mean to visit them
ch is the abbreviation for child

explanation.surface: Begging someone hanging about to go and see a youngster.
explanation.definitionFit: Beseeching means begging or pleading urgently, which is exactly what imploring describes.

clue.text: Extra flexible chaps arriving on time

indicators.note: in a down entry, arriving on the next part means set directly above it

blocks.note: supple means bendy
chaps are men
t is the abbreviation for time

explanation.surface: Bendy gymnasts turning up punctually as additional performers.
explanation.definitionFit: A supplement is an addition such as a newspaper's bonus section, so it is something extra.

clue.text: Become annoyed, having freely agreed ten pounds

indicators.note: letters used freely are not bound to their printed order

blocks.note: all fifteen letters of the phrase

explanation.surface: Someone fuming after readily accepting a ten-pound price.
explanation.walkthrough: Dander is an old word for temper, so getting it up is losing one's temper.
explanation.definitionFit: To get one's dander up is an idiom for losing your temper or growing irritated.

clue.text: Put up in hospital, I lean over and I reject all customary values

definitions.note: the answer describing itself in the first person

indicators.note: in a down entry, putting a word up makes it read from bottom to top

blocks.note: taken as written, then flipped
H is the map symbol for a hospital
the first of the two, taken as written
a ship that lists leans over to one side

explanation.surface: A patient lodged in hospital who leans out of bed and rejects everything.
explanation.definitionFit: Nihilism is the philosophy that rejects all moral and religious principles, so its follower spurns conventional values.

clue.text: It's a bit wet to confuse pair with Dr. No

indicators.note: confusing the letters means mixing them out of order

blocks.note: taken as written
the Bond villain's name, letters only

explanation.surface: A feeble attempt to baffle a couple of agents with a Bond film.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A bit wet' looks like a jibe at a weak person; read literally it is a small piece of wetness. Dr. No is the first James Bond film.
explanation.definitionFit: A single drop of rain is one small piece of the wet stuff falling from the sky.

clue.text: Unrefined hooligan when dancing about

indicators.note: letters dancing about are jigging into a new order

blocks.note: a rough is a rowdy thug
taken as written before being rearranged

explanation.surface: A crude thug cavorting around the dance floor.
explanation.definitionFit: Rough-hewn first meant timber or stone cut but not smoothed; figuratively it means crude or lacking polish.

clue.text: Not fairly matched, but mainly uneventful

indicators.note: mainly means the greater part only, so the tail is cut away

blocks.note: taken as written, then trimmed

explanation.surface: A lopsided contest that was nonetheless dull.
explanation.definitionFit: An uneven contest is one where the sides are unequal, so the match is lopsided.

clue.text: Excellent flatfish!

blocks.note: first meaning: British slang short for brilliant
second meaning: a European sea fish related to the turbot

explanation.walkthrough: The exclamation suggests an angler delighted with a catch; the slang praise and the fish share one spelling.
explanation.definitionFit: Brill is informal British praise meaning brilliant, and also the name of an edible turbot-like fish.

clue.text: Severely scold a bee that has swallowed a rat

indicators.note: something swallowed ends up inside whatever swallowed it

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Telling off an insect that somehow ate a rodent.
explanation.definitionFit: To berate is to tell someone off angrily and at length, a harsh rebuke.

clue.text: Cunning St. Helen's beginning to hold a kind of duck

indicators.note: the beginning of a name is its opening letter
the first pieces hold, or wrap around, the next one

blocks.note: the usual abbreviation for saint
only the initial of the name is kept
the teal is a small freshwater duck

explanation.surface: A sly scheme at the start of St Helens to catch a duck.
explanation.walkthrough: St Helens is a town in north-west England. The duck goes in after the S, splitting ST.
explanation.definitionFit: Stealth is secret, sly action, so it can stand for cunning used as a noun.

clue.text: Get rid of dry white wine

blocks.note: first meaning: to dismiss someone from a job
second meaning: the old name for sherry-like fortified wines from Spain

explanation.surface: Pouring away a disappointing bottle of white.
explanation.walkthrough: Sack is the wine Falstaff drinks in Shakespeare, a dry sherry imported from Spain and the Canaries.
explanation.definitionFit: To sack an employee is to fire them, and sack was also an old name for dry fortified white wine.

clue.text: Sudden growth in business including wine leads to tedium

indicators.note: the first word includes, so holds within it, the second

blocks.note: a boom is a rapid economic upturn
red is a type of wine

explanation.surface: A business boom fuelled by wine turns out to be dull.
explanation.definitionFit: Boredom is the weary state of having nothing interesting to do, the same as tedium.

clue.text: Youth incorporates good and evil spirit

indicators.note: to incorporate is to take something into one's body

blocks.note: a youth is a boy
g is the abbreviation for good

explanation.surface: A young person who is both virtuous and wicked.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Good and evil' reads as a pair of opposites, but 'and' joins the wordplay to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A bogy, also spelled bogey, is a goblin or wicked spirit used to frighten children.

clue.text: He's in the Civil Service. What a game!

indicators.note: one part sits inside the other

blocks.note: taken as written without the apostrophe
standard abbreviation

explanation.surface: Someone exclaiming at a friend's job in government bureaucracy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'What a game!' sounds like scorn for civil service life; only 'game' is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Chess is a strategy board game for two players with kings, queens and pawns.

clue.text: Wee Willie Winkie's dark habit?

blocks.note: night is the dark part of the day
a habit is a garment, such as a gown

explanation.surface: A nursery-rhyme boy and his night-time ways.
explanation.walkthrough: Wee Willie Winkie is a Scottish nursery rhyme figure who 'runs through the town, upstairs and downstairs in his nightgown'. 'Habit' suggests a routine; here it is clothing.
explanation.definitionFit: A nightgown is the loose garment worn to bed, which is what the rhyme's boy runs about in.
